title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
claim: A short finetune that pits a labeled reference loss against a disagreement loss yields a statistic separating in-distribution from shifted batches via a calibrated threshold.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, big arrows between stages, gradient-angle boxes and histogram
description: Three-stage horizontal figure titled 1 Setup, 2 Calibration, 3 Deployment, connected by thick black arrows labeled 'T-step finetune' and '×K on ID eval'. Panel 1 is a feature-space sketch with axes φ1 and φ2. A blue ID manifold blob holds gray support points, blue star anchors and an orange-x eval cluster. A second orange eval blob sits outside it, with arrows marking 'on or off ID manifold'. Panel 2 shows the joint loss formula in blue and orange. Two small boxes compare gradient vectors: a blue ID box where the vectors oppose and λ stays high, and a red OOD box where they are orthogonal and λ drops. Below is a loss-vs-time plot with a blue ID curve ending high and a red OOD curve ending low, plus a 'detection signal' gap. Panel 3 is a histogram of ID calibration λ values with a dashed red threshold q_α. The reject region is shaded pink on the left and labeled flag/keep.
caption: CALD in three steps. (1) Setup. In the PFN’s feature space, a labeled anchor ( ) sits inside the ID manifold; the unlabeled eval batch ( ) arrives with unknown origin — it may sit on or off the ID manifold. (2) Calibration. abstract: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.
